title: A Bottle of Dew — Chapter Summary
intro: A wise king holds up an empty crystal bottle and asks his people: bring the most precious thing in the world. A goldsmith brings gold; a poet brings words; a farmer brings rice; a child brings a single drop of dew. The dew wins — because the present moment, like dew, cannot be saved or repeated. This fable from the unit 'Fables and Folk Tales' teaches us to cherish the NOW.

sections.heading: The Story
bullets: A wise old king gathers his people in the courtyard.
He holds up an empty crystal bottle and asks them to fill it with the 'most precious thing in the world'.
A goldsmith brings gold dust; a poet brings words on paper; a farmer brings a grain of rice.
A child brings a leaf with a single drop of morning dew on it.
The king accepts the dew — because the present moment, like dew, cannot be stored.
The bottle becomes famous; whenever someone forgets to be thankful, they are told 'remember the bottle of dew'.

sections.heading: Vocabulary
bullets: precious — of great value; not common.
thankful — grateful; showing gratitude.
delicately — gently, carefully.
balanced — held without falling.
dew — tiny water drops on grass / leaves in early morning.
courtyard — open space inside / beside a building.
gathered — brought together.
grain — a single small seed of rice / wheat.

sections.heading: Comprehension
bullets: Each character offers what THEY value — gold (wealth), words (lasting beauty), rice (survival), dew (the now).
The four offerings tell us about the four characters as much as about the king's challenge.
The moral — present-moment-as-most-precious — only emerges in the child's offering.
The king's smile is a sign of approval and recognition.
The closing lesson: 'remember the bottle of dew' becomes a proverb in the kingdom.

sections.heading: Language Focus
bullets: COMMON nouns name a class — king, child, bottle, leaf, courtyard.
PROPER nouns name a particular thing and start with a capital — Aesop, Mumbai.
ADJECTIVES describe nouns — wise, old, crystal, small, bright.
Stories are usually told in the PAST tense — gathered, brought, smiled, kept.
Some past-tense forms are regular (-ed): walked, smiled. Others are irregular: bring → brought, see → saw, keep → kept.
Synonyms (precious / valuable; thankful / grateful) and antonyms (precious / worthless) help build vocabulary.

sections.heading: Think and Write
bullets: List five small everyday moments worth being grateful for.
Distinguish a precious OBJECT from a precious MOMENT.
Imagine yourself as the child — describe what you felt when the king smiled.
Continue the story — describe the king walking in the garden the next morning.
Apply the moral to your own life: choose one moment today and live it well.

key_takeaways: A fable carries a moral inside a simple story.
'A Bottle of Dew' teaches that the PRESENT MOMENT is the most precious thing of all.
Each character's offering reflects what they personally value.
Vocabulary: precious, thankful, delicately, balanced, dew, courtyard.
Common vs proper nouns; adjectives; past-tense verbs (regular and irregular).
Connect the moral to your own life — a fable's job is to change how you see the world.

glossary.definition: A short story with a moral lesson, often featuring simple characters or events.
The lesson or message of a story.
A traditional story passed down by word of mouth in a community.
Of great value; treasured; not easily replaced.
Held in such a way that it does not fall.
Tiny water drops that form on grass and leaves in the early morning.
An open space inside or beside a building.
A noun naming a class of things, e.g. king, leaf, child.
A noun naming a particular person, place or thing; always begins with a capital letter.
A word that describes a noun, e.g. wise, crystal, bright.
The verb form used to talk about actions that already happened.
A word that has the same or nearly the same meaning as another word.
A word that has the opposite meaning of another word.
